title: The forgiveness of sins (CCC 976–983)
hook: the Catechism says there is no offense the Church cannot forgive

segments.voice: Yesterday, the laity: clergy, laypeople and religious, different callings in one people. Your line was equal dignity. Did you get to thank someone who serves without a collar? Day one thousand eighty-two.

Near the end of the Apostles' Creed, after the Church and the communion of saints, comes a short line that's easy to say too fast: the forgiveness of sins. It sits in a list with some very large claims, right next to the resurrection of the body and life everlasting. That placement is a clue. The Creed doesn't treat forgiveness as a side topic, a footnote for bad weeks. It puts it among the things a Catholic says they believe about how the whole world is put right. Today the Catechism slows down on that one line, and it makes a bold claim about it.
screen: `A SHORT LINE, SAID FAST.` → `NEXT TO THE RESURRECTION.` → `NOT A FOOTNOTE.`

segments.voice: Start with the room where it began. In John's Gospel, on the evening of Easter, the disciples are behind locked doors. Jesus stands among them, breathes on them, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." The Catechism ties the Creed's line back to that room. It notices that the Creed sets forgiveness alongside the Holy Spirit and the Church, and says they belong together: the Spirit given to the apostles, and the Church sent out with the power to forgive. Second, the doorway. The Catechism calls baptism the first and chief sacrament of forgiveness. In baptism, Catholics believe, sins are washed away completely, and a person starts clean. Third, the second chance. The Catechism admits that baptism doesn't take away human weakness, and the clean start doesn't stay clean. So it turns to the sacrament of penance, confession, for sins committed after baptism. In its later section on confession, it borrows an old picture from early Church writers: after a shipwreck, a plank to hold on to. Fourth, the claim itself. The Catechism says there is no offense, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive. No one, however wicked, should doubt that forgiveness is possible, as long as they are truly sorry. That condition matters. This isn't a promise that sin doesn't count. It's a promise that sorrow is never too late, and that no list of wrongs is too long for mercy to reach. The Catechism adds that Christ wants the door of forgiveness always open to anyone who turns back. Put together, the line in the Creed is less about bookkeeping and more about hope: the claim that a life can be reopened.
screen: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.` · `BAPTISM, THE FIRST FORGIVENESS.` · `A PLANK AFTER THE SHIPWRECK.` · `NO OFFENSE TOO SERIOUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust mercy with one thing. Settle, and breathe slowly. Let one thing come to mind that you've been carrying, something you did, or failed to do, that still sits heavy. Don't replay the whole story. Just name it, quietly, in a few words. Then notice how tightly you're holding it. If you pray, you can hand it over to God, and if you're Catholic, you might decide when you'll bring it to confession. If you don't pray, simply loosen your grip on it for these two minutes, and let it be smaller than you are. The bell holds the time.

The forgiveness of sins. A line of the Creed, joined to the Spirit and the Church: given first in baptism, offered again in confession, and, the Catechism says, closed to no one who is truly sorry. Today's word.
Your line: no sin too big. Today, when an old regret shows up, of yours or someone else's, answer it with the line once, and see what changes. Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the forgiveness of sins in the Creed at Mass, and seek forgiveness for sins after baptism in the sacrament of penance, confessing to a priest and receiving absolution.

original.note: Latin: the forgiveness of sins, as the Apostles' Creed says it in Latin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line in the Creed you say on autopilot.
what it means: Catholics say the Church can forgive any sin for anyone truly sorry: first in baptism, then in confession.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism reads the line with the two before it: the Spirit given on Easter evening, and the Church sent to forgive.

notes: The Catechism is not public domain; every CCC point is paraphrased (976 Creed links forgiveness to the Spirit and the Church; 977 baptism the first and chief sacrament of forgiveness; 980 penance after baptism, with the Fathers' 'plank after shipwreck' image; 982 no offense too serious, for anyone sincerely repentant; the door always open to anyone who turns back). Confirm each paraphrase, and that the shipwreck plank image is fairly placed here (the CCC uses it in this section and in 1446).
Outline hook 'there's no sin the Church can't forgive' reworded in the script's hook field to attribute it to the Catechism and keep the repentance condition.
Original: Latin of the Apostles' Creed, accusative form as it is said in the Creed. Confirm.

Editor pass: unclear 'reads the Creed the same way' rewritten; 'biggest claims' superlative softened; plank-after-shipwreck image now placed in the Catechism's confession section (CCC 1446, added to sources) rather than implied in 976–983; myth item no longer says forgiveness sits 'right after the Church' (the communion of saints comes between); fork reveal no longer claims forgiveness was the first thing Jesus gave (John 20 has 'Peace be to you' first).
